title: 04. BM25 & Lexical Search: The k1 and b Parameters: Tuning BM25
summary: Think of BM25 like a professional camera with two dials: > >; k1 dial = "How much does word frequency matter?" (like ISO sensitivity) >; Turn it to 0: frequency doesn't matter at all — a word present even once is counted >; Turn it up…

sections.title: ① Real-World Analogy
sections.body:
> Think of BM25 like a **professional camera** with two dials:
>
> - **k1 dial** = "How much does word frequency matter?" (like ISO sensitivity)
>   - Turn it to 0: frequency doesn't matter at all — a word present even once is counted
>   - Turn it up high: frequency matters a LOT — very similar to TF-IDF
>   - Middle setting (1.5): balanced — frequency matters, but with diminishing returns
>
> - **b dial** = "How much does document length matter?" (like aperture)
>   - Set to 0: all documents treated the same length — no length penalty
>   - Set to 1: fully normalise by length — short documents heavily favoured
>   - Middle setting (0.75): the most popular real-world default

sections.title: ② Plain English Explanation
sections.body:
BM25 has two parameters you can tune:

**k1** controls the "ceiling" of how much term frequency can boost the score. At k1=0, even a single occurrence gives the max TF score. At k1=100, you need very high counts to approach the ceiling — almost like raw TF-IDF.

**b** controls how aggressively document length is penalised. At b=0, a 10-word document and a 10,000-word document are treated identically. At b=1, the normalisation is full — only the proportion of the document that the word occupies matters.

sections.title: ③ Why Does This Matter?
sections.body: Different domains have different characteristics. In a collection of **tweets** (all short, same length), you might want b=0 because length doesn't vary. In a collection of **legal documents** (lengths vary enormously), you might want b=0.9 to aggressively normalise. Understanding these dials lets you *tune* BM25 for your specific dataset.

sections.title: ④ Step-by-Step Technical Explanation
sections.body:
**How k1 affects the score:**
```
The TF component is: f×(k1+1) / (f + k1)   [simplified when length_factor=1]

When f=1, k1=0:   TF = 1×1 / (1+0)     = 1.0   (max already reached at f=1!)
When f=1, k1=1.5: TF = 1×2.5 / (1+1.5) = 1.0   (same)
When f=5, k1=0:   TF = 5×1 / (5+0)     = 1.0   (no increase! frequency ignored)
When f=5, k1=1.5: TF = 5×2.5 / (5+1.5) = 1.923 (frequency matters!)
When f=5, k1=100: TF = 5×101 / (5+100)  = 4.810 (approaches raw TF)
```

**How b affects the score:**
```
length_factor = 1 - b + b × (|D|/avgdl)

b=0: length_factor = 1 - 0 + 0 × anything = 1.0  (always 1, length ignored)
b=1: length_factor = 0 + 1 × (|D|/avgdl) = |D|/avgdl (full length normalisation)
b=0.75: partial normalisation (the sweet spot)
```

**Practical Guidelines:**

| Domain | Recommended k1 | Recommended b |
|--------|---------------|---------------|
| Web search (default) | 1.2–1.5 | 0.75 |
| Short texts (tweets, titles) | 1.2 | 0.0–0.3 |
| Legal/academic docs (long, varied length) | 1.5–2.0 | 0.9 |
| Titles/headings only | 0.9 | 0.4 |
| Code search | 1.2 | 0.5 |

sections.title: ⑤ Beginner-Friendly Code Example
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- LESSON 8: Tuning k1 and b — Observing the Effects
- EXPERIMENT 1: Effect of k1
- EXPERIMENT 2: Effect of b
- Create artificial documents with very different lengths to show b's effect
- EXPERIMENT 3: Visualise k1 Saturation Curves
- Plot 1: k1 saturation curves
- Length_factor = 1 (doc length = avgdl, so length is neutral)
- Plot 2: b length normalisation curves

**Defines:** `tokenise()`, `bm25_idf()`, `bm25_score()`

```python
# ============================================================
# LESSON 8: Tuning k1 and b — Observing the Effects
# ============================================================

import math
import string
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

documents = [
    "Python is great for machine learning and data science",
    "Java is used for enterprise software development",
    "Python and Java are both popular programming languages",
    "Machine learning requires lots of data and computation",
    "Data science uses Python for statistical analysis and modeling"
]

def tokenise(text):
    text = text.lower()
    text = text.translate(str.maketrans('', '', string.punctuation))
    return text.split()

tokenised_docs = [tokenise(doc) for doc in documents]
N = len(documents)
doc_lengths = [len(tokens) for tokens in tokenised_docs]
avgdl = sum(doc_lengths) / N

df = {}
for tokens in tokenised_docs:
    for word in set(tokens):
        df[word] = df.get(word, 0) + 1

def bm25_idf(word, df, N):
    doc_freq = df.get(word, 0)
    return math.log((N - doc_freq + 0.5) / (doc_freq + 0.5) + 1)

def bm25_score(query, doc_id, tokenised_docs, df, N, doc_lengths, avgdl, k1=1.5, b=0.75):
    query_tokens = tokenise(query)
    total = 0.0
    tokens = tokenised_docs[doc_id]
    doc_len = doc_lengths[doc_id]
    for term in query_tokens:
        f = tokens.count(term)
        if f == 0:
            continue
        idf = bm25_idf(term, df, N)
        length_factor = 1 - b + b * (doc_len / avgdl)
        tf_comp = (f * (k1 + 1)) / (f + k1 * length_factor)
        total += idf * tf_comp
    return total

# ── EXPERIMENT 1: Effect of k1 ────────────────────────────────────────

print("=== EXPERIMENT 1: Effect of k1 (b=0.75 fixed) ===")
print("Query: 'python machine learning data science'")
print()

query = "python machine learning data science"
k1_values = [0.0, 0.5, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0, 5.0, 100.0]

print(f"{'Doc':<6}", end="")
for k1 in k1_values:
    print(f" | {'k1='+str(k1):<10}", end="")
print()
print("-" * (6 + 13 * len(k1_values)))

for doc_id in range(N):
    print(f"Doc {doc_id}", end="")
    for k1 in k1_values:
        score = bm25_score(query, doc_id, tokenised_docs, df, N, doc_lengths, avgdl, k1=k1, b=0.75)
        print(f" | {score:<10.4f}", end="")
    print()

print()
print("Observations:")
print("  k1=0.0: Any doc with the term gets score limited quickly (no frequency benefit)")
print("  k1=1.5: Balanced — frequency helps but has diminishing returns (DEFAULT)")
print("  k1=100: Behaves almost like TF-IDF — frequency keeps helping a lot")
print()

# ── EXPERIMENT 2: Effect of b ─────────────────────────────────────────

print("=== EXPERIMENT 2: Effect of b (k1=1.5 fixed) ===")
print("Query: 'python data'")
print()

# Create artificial documents with very different lengths to show b's effect
long_doc  = " ".join(["Python is used for data science"] * 10)   # ~60 words, lots of repetition
short_doc = "Python data"                                          # 2 words

test_docs = [
    "Python data science",                           # 3 words  (SHORT)
    "Python is used for data analysis and modeling", # 8 words  (MEDIUM)
    long_doc,                                         # ~60 words (LONG)
]
test_tokenised = [tokenise(d) for d in test_docs]
test_lengths = [len(t) for t in test_tokenised]
test_avgdl = sum(test_lengths) / len(test_docs)

test_df = {}
for tokens in test_tokenised:
    for word in set(tokens):
        test_df[word] = test_df.get(word, 0) + 1

b_values = [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]

print(f"Document lengths: {test_lengths}, avgdl={test_avgdl:.1f}")
print()
print(f"{'Doc':<6} {'Length':<8}", end="")
for b in b_values:
    print(f" | {'b='+str(b):<8}", end="")
print()
print("-" * (14 + 11 * len(b_values)))

for doc_id, test_doc in enumerate(test_docs):
    print(f"Doc {doc_id}  {test_lengths[doc_id]:<8}", end="")
    for b in b_values:
        score = bm25_score("python data", doc_id, test_tokenised, test_df,
                           len(test_docs), test_lengths, test_avgdl, k1=1.5, b=b)
        print(f" | {score:<8.4f}", end="")
    print()

print()
print("Observations:")
print("  b=0.0: Long doc scores same as short doc (length ignored)")
print("  b=1.0: Short doc scores MUCH higher (full length normalisation)")
print("  b=0.75: Balanced — short doc slightly favoured (DEFAULT)")

# ── EXPERIMENT 3: Visualise k1 Saturation Curves ─────────────────────

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

# Plot 1: k1 saturation curves
counts = np.arange(0, 31)
for k1 in [0.5, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0, 5.0]:
    # length_factor = 1 (doc length = avgdl, so length is neutral)
    scores = []
    for f in counts:
        if f == 0:
            scores.append(0)
        else:
            scores.append((f * (k1 + 1)) / (f + k1 * 1.0))
    axes[0].plot(counts, scores, label=f'k1={k1}', linewidth=2, marker='o', markersize=3)

axes[0].set_xlabel('Word count in document', fontsize=12)
axes[0].set_ylabel('TF component score', fontsize=12)
axes[0].set_title('Effect of k1 on TF Saturation', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
axes[0].legend()
axes[0].grid(True, alpha=0.3)
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 7)

# Add ceiling annotations
for k1 in [0.5, 1.5, 5.0]:
    ceiling = k1 + 1
    axes[0].axhline(y=ceiling, linestyle='--', alpha=0.3)
    axes[0].text(25, ceiling + 0.1, f'ceiling={ceiling}', fontsize=8)

# Plot 2: b length normalisation curves
doc_lens = np.arange(10, 300, 10)
avg = 100  # avgdl = 100 words
f_fixed = 5  # word appears 5 times

for b in [0.0, 0.25, 0.75, 1.0]:
    scores = []
    for dl in doc_lens:
        lf = 1 - b + b * (dl / avg)
        score = (f_fixed * (1.5 + 1)) / (f_fixed + 1.5 * lf)
        scores.append(score)
    axes[1].plot(doc_lens, scores, label=f'b={b}', linewidth=2)

axes[1].axvline(x=avg, color='gray', linestyle='--', label=f'avgdl={avg}')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Document length (words)', fontsize=12)
axes[1].set_ylabel('TF component score (word appears 5×)', fontsize=12)
axes[1].set_title('Effect of b on Length Normalisation', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
axes[1].legend()
axes[1].grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('bm25_k1_b_effects.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()
print("\nPlot saved as 'bm25_k1_b_effects.png'")
```

**Expected Output (excerpt):**
```
=== EXPERIMENT 1: Effect of k1 (b=0.75 fixed) ===

Doc    | k1=0.0     | k1=0.5     | k1=1.2     | k1=1.5     | k1=2.0     | k1=5.0     | k1=100.0
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Doc 0  | 1.4059     | 1.8241     | 2.0906     | 2.1849     | 2.3073     | 2.7412     | 3.4913
Doc 3  | 1.6209     | 1.9849     | 2.1805     | 2.2318     | 2.2997     | 2.5432     | 2.9183
Doc 4  | 0.4859     | 0.6473     | 0.7526     | 0.7908     | 0.8458     | 1.0456     | 1.3795

=== EXPERIMENT 2: Effect of b (k1=1.5 fixed) ===

Doc    Length   | b=0.0    | b=0.25   | b=0.5    | b=0.75   | b=1.0
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Doc 0  3        | 2.2761   | 2.4210   | 2.5866   | 2.7754   | 2.9912
Doc 1  8        | 2.2761   | 2.2386   | 2.2007   | 2.1624   | 2.1237
Doc 2  60       | 2.2761   | 1.8219   | 1.4760   | 1.2148   | 1.0157
```

sections.title: ⑥ Common Beginner Mistakes
sections.body:
❌ **Mistake 1:** Setting b=1.0 for long-document collections — severely penalises relevant long docs
✅ **Fix:** Start with b=0.75 and tune experimentally; b=1.0 is rarely optimal

❌ **Mistake 2:** Setting k1=0 and wondering why all matching docs have the same score
✅ **Fix:** k1=0 makes BM25 binary — presence/absence only, no frequency benefit

❌ **Mistake 3:** Not tuning k1 and b for your domain, just using defaults blindly
✅ **Fix:** Run experiments with different values on your actual data and measure retrieval quality

❌ **Mistake 4:** Thinking there's one universally best k1 and b
✅ **Fix:** They depend on your corpus — there is no universal answer

❌ **Mistake 5:** Confusing b=0 (ignore length) with b=1 (full normalisation)
✅ **Fix:** Think of b as a dial: 0=off, 1=maximum normalisation

sections.title: ⑦ Quick Recap
sections.body:
- 🎛️ **k1** = TF saturation speed. Low → saturates fast. High → like TF-IDF. Default=1.5
- 📏 **b** = Length normalisation strength. 0 → ignore length. 1 → full normalisation. Default=0.75
- 🏁 BM25 score ceiling for TF component = **k1 + 1** (never exceeded)
- 🩺 Tune k1 higher for collections where frequency *really matters*
- ⚖️ Tune b lower for collections where all docs are approximately the same length
